title: Physics 121
description: The whole Mechanics Blueprint: measurement and units, 1D motion, vectors, calculus, projectiles, momentum and impulse, forces and friction, circular motion and gravity, rotation and torque, energy, and equilibrium.

cards.definition: The digits in a measurement that were actually measured (plus one estimated digit).
Zeros before the first nonzero digit (0.004). Never significant: they only place the decimal point.
Zeros between nonzero digits (1005). Always significant.
Zeros at the end. Significant only if the number has a decimal point: 190 has 2, 190. has 3, 190.0 has 4.
A number as (1 to 10) × 10ⁿ. The mantissa shows exactly the sig figs: 0.0500 = 5.00 × 10⁻².
Means the number is smaller than 1: 10⁻³ moves the decimal point 3 places left.
A fraction equal to 1, like (1000 m / 1 km). The unit you want to cancel goes on the bottom.
Multiply by conversion factors and cross out units until only the unit you want is left. No units, no points!
Revenue − costs. Negative profit is a loss. A rate cost ($/day) must be multiplied by the time first.
Meter, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela. Everything else (N, J, W) is built from them.
Change in position, x_final − x_initial. Has a direction (sign).
Total path length traveled. Never negative; ≥ |displacement|.
Rate of change of position (m/s), with a sign for direction.
Rate of change of velocity: a = Δv / Δt (m/s²). Its sign is a direction, not "speeding up".
v and a with the same sign: speeding up. Opposite signs: slowing down.
Total displacement ÷ total time. With constant acceleration it also equals (v₀ + v)/2.
Total distance ÷ total time. Differs from |average velocity| when the object turns around.
Final velocity after accelerating for time t (constant a).
Displacement after time t with constant a (no final velocity needed).
Links speeds and displacement with no time needed.
Displacement = average velocity × time, for constant acceleration.
Velocity. Straight line = constant velocity; curve = accelerating.
Slope = acceleration; area under the line = displacement (negative below the axis).
A vector has magnitude AND direction (displacement, velocity). A scalar has only size (distance, speed, time).
Ax = A cos θ, Ay = A sin θ when θ is measured from the +x axis. Signs come from the quadrant.
|R| = √(Rx² + Ry²), after adding all the x-components and all the y-components.
Direction measured counterclockwise from +x (East), 0° to 360°.
Start pointing West, rotate θ toward North. Polar angle 180° − θ.
tan⁻¹(Ry/Rx) only returns −90° to 90°. If Rx < 0, add 180°. Always sketch the triangle.
The single vector equal to the sum of the others: tip-to-tail, or add the components.
Rate of change. v = dx/dt, a = dv/dt. Power rule: d/dt(tⁿ) = n·tⁿ⁻¹.
Area under the curve, the reverse of a derivative: ∫tⁿ dt = tⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C, and C is the starting value.
2D motion where a_x = 0 and a_y = −9.8 m/s². Solve x and y as two 1D problems linked by time.
The quantity that ends the motion (a fall height, a wall distance). Use it to find t, then use t in the other direction.
p = mv, a vector (kg·m/s). Conserved in any collision of a closed system.
Objects stick: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v_f. Momentum kept, kinetic energy lost.
Objects bounce and kinetic energy is conserved too: two equations, two unknown final velocities.
J = FΔt = Δp (N·s = kg·m/s). For a changing force, it is the area under the F-t graph.
F_net = ma (also F = Δp/Δt). Add all external forces as vectors first.
|f| = μ·F_N, parallel to the surface. Static: up to μs·F_N, matching the push. Kinetic (sliding): μk·F_N.
A surface's push perpendicular to itself. mg on a level floor, mg cos θ on a ramp.
a = v²/r, pointing to the center. Constant speed in a circle is still acceleration.
F = Gm₁m₂/r², G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². r is center to center.
Gravity is the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r).
x→θ, v→ω, a→α, m→I, F→τ, p = mv → L = Iω. Same kinematics equations, angles in radians.
|τ| = rF sin θ (N·m), the rotational "force". τ_net = Iα.
The rotational "mass": depends on mass AND how far it sits from the axis. Rod (center) mL²/12, rod (end) mL²/3, ring mr², sphere ⅖mr².
KE = ½mv² (joules). A scalar.
Gravity: mgh (h above your chosen zero). Spring: ½kx² (x = stretch or squeeze).
KE₀ + PE₀ = KE_f + PE_f, minus any work friction does (μk·F_N·d). Energy is moved around, never made or destroyed.
Σ F = 0 and Σ τ = 0. Pick the pivot point to make unknown forces drop out of the torque sum.

questions.prompt: Which zeros in 0.04080 are significant?
choices: The zero between the 4 and 8, and the final zero
Only the zero between the 4 and 8
questions.answer: The zero between the 4 and 8, and the final zero
questions.explanation: Leading zeros (0.0…) only place the decimal point. The captive zero counts, and the trailing zero counts because there is a decimal point: 4 sig figs.

questions.prompt: One lab notebook says 2300 m and another says 2300. m. How many sig figs does each have?
questions.explanation: Without a decimal point the trailing zeros are placeholders (2 sig figs). The written decimal point says they were measured (4).

questions.prompt: Why would someone write 600. g with a decimal point at the end?
choices: To show all three digits were measured: 3 sig figs
It is a typo for 600.0 g
It means the mass was rounded to the nearest 100 g
questions.answer: To show all three digits were measured: 3 sig figs
questions.explanation: 600 alone has 1 sig fig. The trailing point makes the zeros count, so 600. has 3 (and 600.0 would have 4).

questions.prompt: How many significant figures does 0.00905 have?
questions.explanation: The three leading zeros never count; 9, the captive 0 and 5 do: 3.

questions.prompt: How many significant figures does 7020. have?
questions.explanation: Captive zero counts, and the trailing zero counts because of the decimal point: 4.

questions.prompt: How many significant figures does 50,000 have (no decimal point)?
questions.explanation: With no decimal point, trailing zeros are placeholders: only the 5 counts. Write 5.0000 × 10⁴ if all five were measured.

questions.prompt: How many significant figures does 0.300 have?
questions.explanation: The leading 0 doesn't count; the 3 and both trailing zeros after the decimal point do: 3.

questions.prompt: Which pair shows the same value AND the same number of sig figs?
questions.explanation: 0.00720 has 3 sig figs (the trailing 0 counts) and is smaller than 1, so the power is negative: 7.20 × 10⁻³. 720 has only 2.

questions.prompt: A length is about four thousand meters, measured to the nearest 10 m (3 sig figs). How should you write it?
questions.explanation: 4000 shows only 1 sig fig. Scientific notation lets the mantissa carry exactly the 3 measured digits: 4.00.

questions.prompt: Which number is the largest?
questions.explanation: Compare powers first: 10⁻² beats 10⁻³, so 3.1 × 10⁻² = 0.031 wins even though 9.8 has a bigger mantissa.

questions.prompt: When 0.000607 is written in scientific notation, what is the power of ten?
questions.explanation: 0.000607 = 6.07 × 10⁻⁴: the decimal point moves 4 places right to get past the 6, so the power is −4.

questions.prompt: Round 0.0046350 to 2 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Start counting at the 4 (leading zeros don't count): 4, 6, and the next digit is 3, so round down to 0.0046. "0.00" is 2 decimal places.

questions.prompt: Converting 90 km/h to m/s, a student gets 324 m/s. What went wrong?
choices: They multiplied by 3.6 instead of dividing
They forgot to convert hours to minutes
They should have multiplied by 1000 only
questions.answer: They multiplied by 3.6 instead of dividing
questions.explanation: 90 × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 h / 3600 s) = 25 m/s. 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h, so km/h → m/s divides by 3.6.

questions.prompt: Which product comes out in years?
questions.explanation: Cross out units: gems cancel gem, months cancel months, leaving years (15 years). The others leave gems²/year, gems²/month and months²/(gem·year).

questions.prompt: A snail crawls at 1.5 mm/s. How many meters does it cover in one hour?
questions.explanation: 1.5 mm/s × (1 m / 1000 mm) × (3600 s / 1 h) × 1 h = 5.4 m. Forgetting mm → m gives 5400.

questions.prompt: A resting heart beats 72 times per minute. How many beats is that in one day?
questions.explanation: 72 beats/min × 60 min/h × 24 h/day = 103,680 beats. Stopping at 4,320 gives beats per hour.

questions.prompt: A hummingbird flies at 13 m/s. What is that in km/h?
A laptop costs $1,360. You earn $12 per hour of work, but $3 of every hour goes to bus fare. How many whole hours must you work to afford it?
questions.explanation: You keep $12 − $3 = $9/h. $1,360 × (1 h / $9) = 151.1 h; 151 hours leaves you short, so 152.

questions.prompt: A lab grows one sapphire every 4 months (use 30 days per month). The machine's electricity costs $6 per day, and each sapphire sells for $2,500. What is the profit per sapphire?
questions.explanation: Electricity: $6/day × 120 days = $720. Profit = $2,500 − $720 = $1,780. Leaving out the cost answers a different question (revenue).

questions.prompt: Each lab-grown sapphire earns you $1,780 profit and takes 4 months to make, one at a time; you can only sell whole ones. How many years until you can afford a $27,000 boat?
questions.explanation: $27,000 ÷ $1,780 = 15.2 → 16 sapphires (15 is not enough). 16 × 4 months × (1 year / 12 months) = 5.33 years. Using the $2,500 sale price instead of the profit is the trap.

questions.prompt: A fish tank heater costs $0.35 per day to run. What does it cost over a 365-day year?
Making one item costs $9/day for 200 days, and it sells for $1,500. What happens?
questions.explanation: Cost per item: $9/day × 200 days = $1,800. Profit = $1,500 − $1,800 = −$300, a loss.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the seven SI base units?
questions.explanation: The base units are meter, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Newtons, joules and watts are derived from them.

questions.prompt: A newton is a derived unit. What is it in base units?
questions.explanation: F = ma: kilograms times m/s². kg·m/s is momentum and kg·m²/s² is a joule.

questions.prompt: A marathon is 26.2 miles. How many kilometers is that? (1 km = 0.6214 mi)
questions.explanation: Put miles on the bottom so they cancel: 26.2 mi × (1 km / 0.6214 mi) = 42.16 km. Multiplying by 0.6214 gives the wrong direction.

questions.prompt: Gold is priced per troy ounce (31.10 g), not the everyday ounce (28.35 g). How many troy ounces are in 1 kg of gold?
questions.explanation: 1000 g × (1 troy oz / 31.10 g) = 32.15 troy oz. The blueprint's gold example uses 35.27 oz/kg, which is the everyday ounce, so it overcounts the gold's value by about 10%.

questions.prompt: A runner does 3 full laps of a 400 m track and stops exactly at the starting line. What are the distance and the displacement?
questions.explanation: Distance counts every meter run (3 × 400). Displacement only compares start and finish, which are the same spot.

questions.prompt: An object has a negative acceleration. Which MUST be true?
choices: Its velocity is changing toward the negative direction
It is moving in the negative direction
questions.answer: Its velocity is changing toward the negative direction
questions.explanation: A negative a only says v is getting more negative. If v is negative too, the object is actually speeding up.

questions.prompt: Take West as negative. A truck is moving West and slowing down. What are the signs?
questions.explanation: Moving West: v < 0. Slowing down means a points opposite to v, so a > 0 even though it's "decelerating".

questions.prompt: A ball rolled up a ramp stops for an instant at its highest point before rolling back. At that instant…
choices: both v and a are at their maximum
questions.explanation: The velocity is passing through zero (changing from + to −), so it is still changing: a ≠ 0. a = 0 would leave it stuck at rest.

questions.prompt: On a velocity-vs-time graph, what do the slope and the area under the line tell you?
questions.explanation: Slope = Δv/Δt (acceleration). Area = v × t (displacement; area below the axis counts negative).

questions.prompt: A position-vs-time graph is a straight line sloping downward. The object is…
choices: moving in the − direction at constant speed
questions.answer: moving in the − direction at constant speed
questions.explanation: Slope of x-vs-t is velocity. A straight line has one constant slope; sloping down means that velocity is negative.

questions.prompt: During a stretch where a car holds a steady −20 m/s, what does the acceleration-vs-time graph show?
choices: A flat line at some negative value
questions.explanation: Constant velocity, even a negative one, means no change in v: a = 0. The −20 shows on the v-vs-t graph, not the a-vs-t graph.

questions.prompt: You drive 60 km at 30 km/h, then another 60 km at 60 km/h. What is your average speed?
questions.explanation: Times: 2 h + 1 h = 3 h for 120 km, so 40 km/h. Averaging the speeds (45) ignores that you spent longer at the slow speed.

questions.prompt: Take East as positive. A train moving East at 25 m/s slows to 10 m/s in 6 s. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: a = (v − v₀)/t = (10 − 25)/6 = −2.5 m/s². Slowing down while moving + gives a negative a.

questions.prompt: Take East as positive. A puck sliding West at 12 m/s is hit and 0.5 s later slides East at 8 m/s. What was its average acceleration?
questions.explanation: a = (v − v₀)/t = (+8 − (−12))/0.5 = 40 m/s². Using 8 − 12 forgets that the velocity changed direction.

questions.prompt: Take North as positive. A bus moving North goes from +8 m/s to +20 m/s in 4 s, holds +20 m/s for 240 m, then brakes to a stop in 6 s. How long does the whole trip take?
questions.explanation: The middle part needs t = Δx / v = 240/20 = 12 s. Total: 4 + 12 + 6 = 22 s.

questions.prompt: Take North as positive. A bus moving North goes from +8 m/s to +20 m/s in 4 s, holds +20 m/s for 240 m, then brakes to a stop in 6 s. What is its total displacement?
questions.explanation: Speeding up: average 14 m/s × 4 s = 56 m. Cruising: 240 m. Braking: average 10 m/s × 6 s = 60 m. Total 356 m. Using the final speeds (80 + 120) overcounts.

questions.prompt: Take North as positive. A bus moving North goes from +8 m/s to +20 m/s in 4 s, holds +20 m/s for 240 m, then brakes to a stop in 6 s. What is its average velocity for the whole trip?
questions.explanation: Total displacement / total time = 356 m / 22 s = 16.2 m/s. Averaging 8, 20 and 0 gives a meaningless number.

questions.prompt: Take West as negative. A car starts from rest and reaches −30 m/s while moving −90 m. How long does that take?
questions.explanation: Average velocity = (0 + (−30))/2 = −15 m/s, so t = −90 / −15 = 6 s. Dividing by the final −30 m/s gives 3 s, as if it had been at full speed the whole time.

questions.prompt: Take West as negative. A car speeds up steadily from rest to −30 m/s over a displacement of −90 m. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: v² = v₀² + 2aΔx → a = 900 / (2 × −90) = −5 m/s². It speeds up while moving −, so a is negative.

questions.prompt: A cart is pushed up a ramp at +6 m/s and has a constant acceleration of −2 m/s² (it slows, stops, and rolls back). What is its displacement after 5 s?
questions.explanation: Δx = v₀t + ½at² = 30 − 25 = 5 m. The formula handles the turnaround automatically.

questions.prompt: A cart is pushed up a ramp at +6 m/s and has a constant acceleration of −2 m/s², so it slows, stops, and rolls back down. What total DISTANCE does it travel in the first 5 s?
questions.explanation: It stops at t = 3 s after going up 6²/(2·2) = 9 m, then rolls back ½·2·2² = 4 m in the last 2 s: 9 + 4 = 13 m. The displacement is only 5 m.

questions.prompt: A velocity-vs-time graph is flat at −15 m/s from t = 0 to 4 s, then a straight line up to 0 m/s at t = 10 s. What is the displacement from 0 to 10 s?
questions.explanation: Rectangle: −15 × 4 = −60 m. Triangle: ½ × (−15) × 6 = −45 m. Total −105 m (below the axis, so negative).

questions.prompt: A car moving at 28 m/s brakes steadily to a stop in 70 m. How long does it take to stop?
questions.explanation: Average velocity while braking = 28/2 = 14 m/s; t = 70 / 14 = 5 s.

questions.prompt: Take East as positive. A plane holds −220 m/s (heading West). How long does it take to cover a displacement of −33,000 m?
questions.explanation: t = Δx / v = −33,000 / −220 = 150 s. The negatives cancel; time is always positive.

questions.prompt: East is positive. A cyclist starts from rest and reaches 16 m/s in 20 s, rides at 16 m/s for 160 m, then brakes steadily to a stop over 400 m. How long does the whole trip take?
questions.explanation: Each acceleration change is a new problem: 20 s, then 160/16 = 10 s, then Δx = ½(v₀ + v)t → t = 2(400)/16 = 50 s: 80 s total. (The blueprint's v-t graph for its own trip of this kind labels the end at 100 s, but its parts add up to 120 s.)

questions.prompt: What does "25° North of West" mean?
choices: Point West, then turn 25° toward North
Point North, then turn 25° toward West
Point West, then turn 25° toward South
questions.answer: Point West, then turn 25° toward North
questions.explanation: Read it backwards: start at the last direction (West), rotate toward the first (North).

questions.prompt: What is the polar angle (counterclockwise from East) of a vector pointing 25° North of West?
questions.explanation: West is 180°; turning 25° toward North (back toward 90°) gives 180° − 25° = 155°. 205° would be 25° South of West.

questions.prompt: A vector points 30° East of North. Which component uses cos 30°?
questions.explanation: cos goes with the side next to the angle. The 30° is measured from North, so North (y) gets cos and East (x) gets sin.

questions.prompt: R has Rx = −12 and Ry = −5. Your calculator says tan⁻¹(Ry/Rx) = 22.6°. What is R's actual polar angle?
questions.explanation: Both components are negative, so R is in the 3rd quadrant. tan⁻¹ can't see that (−5/−12 = 5/12), so add 180°.

questions.prompt: When does |A + B| equal |A| + |B|?
choices: Only when A and B point in the same direction
When A and B are perpendicular
When A and B point in opposite directions
questions.answer: Only when A and B point in the same direction
questions.explanation: Magnitudes only add straight up when nothing cancels. Perpendicular gives √(A² + B²); opposite gives |A − B|.

questions.prompt: Does A + B + C equal C + A + B?
choices: Yes: the order doesn't change the resultant
No: the first vector sets the direction
Only if they are all the same length
Only if none of them point West
questions.answer: Yes: the order doesn't change the resultant
questions.explanation: Adding vectors means adding their components, and ordinary addition doesn't care about order.

questions.prompt: What is −A compared to A?
questions.explanation: Flip both components' signs: the arrow turns around but keeps its length. That's how A − B = A + (−B) works.

questions.prompt: You walk 12 m North, then 5 m West. How far are you from where you started?
questions.explanation: √(12² + 5²) = 13 m. Adding 12 + 5 = 17 m gives the distance walked, not the displacement.

questions.prompt: You walk 12 m North, then 5 m West. What is the polar angle of your displacement (counterclockwise from East)?
Add three vectors: A = 20 m due East, B = 30 m at 40° North of West, C = 15 m due South. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
Add three vectors: A = 20 m due East, B = 30 m at 40° North of West, C = 15 m due South. The resultant points θ° North of West. What is θ?
questions.explanation: Rx is negative and Ry positive (North of West). θ = tan⁻¹(|Ry|/|Rx|) = tan⁻¹(4.28/2.98) = 55.2°, i.e. polar 124.8°.

questions.prompt: A 50 m displacement points 35° West of South. What is its y-component (North = +y)?
questions.explanation: The 35° is measured from South, so the South part uses cos: 50 cos 35° = 40.96 m, negative because it points South.

questions.prompt: A = 10 m due East and B = 10 m due North. What is the magnitude of A − B?
questions.explanation: A − B = A + (−B) = (10, 0) + (0, −10) = (10, −10), magnitude √200 = 14.14 m. It is not 0: the vectors point different ways.

questions.prompt: R = (−9 m, +14 m). It points θ° North of West. What is θ?
questions.explanation: Measured from the West axis: tan θ = |Ry| / |Rx| = 14/9, θ = 57.3°. Using 9/14 gives 32.7°, the angle from North.

questions.prompt: A resultant is √1300 m. What is that to 4 significant figures?
questions.explanation: √1300 = 36.0555…, and the 5 after the 36.05 rounds it up to 36.06. (The blueprint's Example 15 writes 36.05, which drops the digit instead of rounding.)

questions.prompt: Velocity is the ___ of position with respect to time.
questions.explanation: v = dx/dt: how fast position changes. Going the other way, integrating velocity gives back position.

questions.prompt: On a v-t graph, what does the area under the curve between t₁ and t₂ give?
choices: The displacement between t₁ and t₂
questions.answer: The displacement between t₁ and t₂
questions.explanation: Area = ∫v dt = Δx. The slope of the v-t graph is the acceleration.

questions.prompt: Integrating v(t) gives x(t) plus a constant. What does that constant stand for?
questions.explanation: At t = 0 every t term vanishes and only the constant is left, so it is x(0) = x₀. Integrating a(t) the same way leaves v₀.

questions.prompt: x(t) = 4t² − 3t + 2 (meters, seconds). What kind of motion is this?
questions.explanation: v(t) = 8t − 3 and a(t) = 8: constant. The t² coefficient is ½a, not a, which is where Δx = v₀t + ½at² comes from.

questions.prompt: x(t) = 3t⁴ − 2t² + 5 (meters, t in seconds). What is the velocity at t = 2 s?
x(t) = 3t⁴ − 2t² + 5 (meters, t in seconds). What is the acceleration at t = 1 s?
questions.explanation: v(t) = 12t³ − 4t, then a(t) = 36t² − 4: a(1) = 32 m/s².

questions.prompt: v(t) = 6t² + 4 (m/s), and the object is at x = 0 when t = 0. Where is it at t = 3 s?
a(t) = 12t (m/s², t in seconds), and v = 5 m/s at t = 0. What is v at t = 2 s?
questions.explanation: v(t) = 6t² + v₀ = 6t² + 5, so v(2) = 29 m/s. Forgetting the +5 gives 24.

questions.prompt: v(t) = 3t² − 12 (m/s). At what time t > 0 is the object momentarily at rest?
questions.explanation: Set v = 0: 3t² = 12, t = 2 s. That is where x(t) turns around.

questions.prompt: In a projectile problem, which quantity do the x and y parts share?
questions.explanation: x and y are two separate 1D problems (a_x = 0, a_y = −9.8 m/s²). Only t is the same in both, which is why you solve for t in one and use it in the other.

questions.prompt: Ignoring air resistance, what is a projectile's horizontal acceleration?
choices: It depends on the launch angle
questions.explanation: Gravity only pulls down, so v_x never changes. −9.8 m/s² is a_y.

questions.prompt: At the very top of its path, a ball launched at an angle has:
choices: v_x = 0, but v_y is at its largest
questions.explanation: It stops rising, so v_y = 0, but it is still moving sideways at v_x. Gravity is still acting, so a_y = −9.8 m/s² at the top too.

questions.prompt: One ball is dropped and another is fired horizontally from the same height at the same instant. Which lands first? (no air resistance)
choices: They land at the same time
It depends on how fast the fired ball goes
questions.answer: They land at the same time
questions.explanation: Both start with v_y = 0 and fall the same height with the same a_y, so the y problem (and the time) is identical. The horizontal speed only changes where it lands.

questions.prompt: Launched from level ground at the same speed, which angle gives the same range as 30°?
questions.explanation: Range depends on sin(2θ), and sin 60° = sin 120°: complementary angles (30° and 60°) land in the same spot. 45° goes farthest.

questions.prompt: A ball rolls off a 31.4 m high roof at 12 m/s horizontally. How long is it in the air? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Only the fall matters for time: −31.4 = ½(−9.8)t² → t = 2.53 s. The 12 m/s is horizontal.

questions.prompt: A marble rolls off a 1.2 m high table at 2.5 m/s. How far from the table's edge does it land? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A soccer ball is kicked from the ground at 18 m/s, 50° above the horizontal. How high does it go? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A soccer ball is kicked from level ground at 18 m/s, 50° above the horizontal. How long is it in the air? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.explanation: It lands when Δy = 0: 0 = v₀y t − 4.9t², so t = 2v₀y/9.8 = 2(13.79)/9.8 = 2.81 s.

questions.prompt: A dart is thrown from ground level at 25 m/s, 20° above the horizontal, at a wall 30 m away. How high up the wall does it hit? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Δx is the limiting factor: t = 30/(25 cos 20°) = 1.277 s. Δy = (25 sin 20°)t − 4.9t² = 2.93 m. (Carry the digits: the blueprint's Spider-Man example, done the same way, comes out to 7.74 m, not 7.69 m.)

questions.prompt: Why does momentum have a direction?
choices: It is mass × velocity, and velocity is a vector
It doesn't: momentum is a scalar
questions.answer: It is mass × velocity, and velocity is a vector
questions.explanation: p = mv. Mass is a scalar, so p points wherever v points; moving left means negative momentum.

questions.prompt: When is the total momentum of a system conserved?
choices: When no net outside force acts on it (a closed system)
Only when the objects stick together
Only when both start at rest
questions.answer: When no net outside force acts on it (a closed system)
questions.explanation: Inside forces during a collision cancel in pairs, so momentum is conserved in every collision of a closed system, elastic or not.

questions.prompt: Two carts collide and stick together. What happens to their total kinetic energy?
choices: Some of it is lost (to heat, sound, bending)
questions.answer: Some of it is lost (to heat, sound, bending)
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved, kinetic energy isn't: that is what "inelastic" means. Only elastic collisions keep KE.

questions.prompt: Which unit is the same as 1 N·s?
questions.explanation: N = kg·m/s², times s gives kg·m/s: impulse and momentum have the same units, since J = Δp.

questions.prompt: An airbag makes your head stop over a longer time. Why does that help?
choices: Same change in momentum, so a longer Δt means a smaller force
It reduces your change in momentum
questions.answer: Same change in momentum, so a longer Δt means a smaller force
questions.explanation: You go from moving to stopped either way, so J = Δp is fixed. J = FΔt: stretch Δt and F shrinks.

questions.prompt: A 1500 kg car going East at 20 m/s rear-ends a 2500 kg truck at rest, and they lock together. What is their velocity right after? (East = +)
questions.explanation: 30,000 kg·m/s before = (4000 kg)v after, so v = 7.5 m/s.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg puck moving right at 4 m/s and a 2 kg puck moving left at 6 m/s collide and stick. What is their velocity after? (right = +)
questions.explanation: (3)(4) + (2)(−6) = 0, so the stuck pair stops dead: 0 m/s. The left-moving puck's momentum is negative.

questions.prompt: A 0.145 kg baseball comes in at 40 m/s (moving left) and leaves the bat at 50 m/s (moving right). What impulse does the bat give it? (right = +)
questions.explanation: J = Δp = (0.145)(+50) − (0.145)(−40) = 13.05 N·s. Using 50 − 40 forgets that the ball reversed direction.

questions.prompt: The bat in a hit gives a baseball an impulse of 13.05 N·s over 0.0015 s. What is the average force?
A 4 kg cart moving East at 6 m/s and a 2 kg cart moving North at 9 m/s collide and stick. How fast do they move afterward?
questions.explanation: Do x and y separately: p_x = 24, p_y = 18 kg·m/s, so p = 30 kg·m/s and v = 30/6 = 5 m/s.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg ball moving right at 6 m/s hits a 6 kg ball at rest head-on, elastically. What is the 2 kg ball's velocity after? (right = +)
questions.explanation: v₁f = (m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂)·v₁ = (−4/8)(6) = −3 m/s: the lighter ball bounces back.

questions.prompt: A 30 kg box stays still while you push it sideways with 50 N. The max static friction μs·mg is 120 N. How big is the friction force right now?
questions.explanation: Static friction matches the push exactly, up to its limit. μs·mg = 120 N is the most it can give, not what it always gives.

questions.prompt: Why is μs usually bigger than μk for the same surfaces?
choices: It takes more force to start something sliding than to keep it sliding
Kinetic friction only acts on light objects
questions.answer: It takes more force to start something sliding than to keep it sliding
questions.explanation: Once it slides, kinetic friction (μk·F_N) takes over and is smaller, which is why a heavy box gets easier to push once it starts moving.

questions.prompt: A book rests on a table and you press down on it. What happens to the normal force?
questions.explanation: The table pushes back on everything pressing into it: F_N = mg + your push. More normal force means more friction too.

questions.prompt: A box slides to the right across a floor. On its free-body diagram, which way does kinetic friction point?
questions.explanation: Friction is parallel to the surface and opposes the sliding. Weight points down and the normal force up.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg block and a 20 kg block slide down the same ramp with the same μk. Which accelerates faster?
questions.explanation: a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ): every force here is proportional to m, so m drops out.

questions.prompt: A 25 kg crate on frictionless ice is pulled East with 120 N and West with 45 N. What is its acceleration? (East = +)
questions.explanation: F_net = 120 − 45 = 75 N, so a = 75/25 = 3 m/s² East.

questions.prompt: A 40 kg dresser sits on a floor with μs = 0.45. What push is needed to start it sliding? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
You push the same 40 kg dresser (μk = 0.30) with 250 N and it slides. What is its acceleration? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Kinetic friction: 0.30 × 40 × 9.8 = 117.6 N. F_net = 132.4 N, a = 3.31 m/s².

questions.prompt: A 12 kg sled slides down a frictionless 25° hill. What is its acceleration? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Only mg sin 25° acts along the slope: a = 9.8 sin 25° = 4.14 m/s². The mass cancels.

questions.prompt: An 8 kg puck on frictionless ice is pushed with 30 N East and 40 N North at the same time. What is the size of its acceleration?
questions.explanation: Add forces as vectors: √(30² + 40²) = 50 N, so a = 50/8 = 6.25 m/s². 70/8 adds them as if they were in a line.

questions.prompt: A 600 kg go-kart at 10 m/s slides across a 4 m strip with μk = 0.5, then onto gravel with μk = 0.8. How far into the gravel does it slide? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Strip: a = −4.9 m/s², v² = 100 − 2(4.9)(4) = 60.8. Gravel: a = −7.84 m/s², Δx = 60.8/(2·7.84) = 3.88 m. Keep v² unrounded: the blueprint's F1 example rounds √24.8 = 4.98 m/s down to 4.9 and gets 1.36 m instead of 1.41 m.

questions.prompt: A car drives around a circle at a constant 15 m/s. Is it accelerating?
questions.explanation: Velocity is speed and direction, so turning is accelerating: a = v²/r, toward the center.

questions.prompt: Which way does centripetal acceleration point?
choices: Toward the center of the circle
questions.answer: Toward the center of the circle
questions.explanation: It is always perpendicular to the velocity, pointing to the center: that is what bends the path.

questions.prompt: What supplies the centripetal force for a car on a flat curve?
choices: Friction between the tires and the road
questions.answer: Friction between the tires and the road
questions.explanation: Centripetal force is a job, not a new force: on a flat road friction does it (on ice, the car goes straight).

questions.prompt: If the distance between two planets doubles, the gravitational force between them becomes:
questions.explanation: F = Gm₁m₂/d²: doubling d makes d² four times bigger, so F is a quarter.

questions.prompt: Does a satellite's own mass change the speed it needs for a given circular orbit?
choices: No: it cancels from GMm/r² = mv²/r
questions.answer: No: it cancels from GMm/r² = mv²/r
questions.explanation: m appears on both sides, so v = √(GM/r) depends only on the planet's mass and the orbit radius.

questions.prompt: A kid rides the edge of a merry-go-round, 2.5 m from the center, at 3 m/s. What is the kid's centripetal acceleration?
questions.explanation: a = v²/r = 3²/2.5 = 3.6 m/s², toward the center.

questions.prompt: A 1200 kg car rounds a curve of radius 80 m at 25 m/s. How much sideways force does the road supply?
A string breaks above 40 N. What is the fastest a 0.5 kg ball can whirl on it in a horizontal circle of radius 1.2 m (frictionless table)?
The Moon (7.35 × 10²² kg) is 3.84 × 10⁸ m from Earth (5.97 × 10²⁴ kg). What is the gravitational force between them? (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
questions.explanation: F = Gm₁m₂/d² = 1.98 × 10²⁰ N. Remember to square the distance.

questions.prompt: A space station orbits 6.78 × 10⁶ m from Earth's center (Earth: 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg). How fast does it move? (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
questions.explanation: GMm/r² = mv²/r → v = √(GM/r) = 7664 m/s. (Same method for Earth around the Sun: the blueprint's Example 19 numbers give a period of about 363 days, not 362.)

questions.prompt: The rotational kinematics equations (Δθ = ω₀t + ½αt² etc.) need angles in:
choices: any unit, as long as you're consistent
questions.explanation: They come from s = rθ, which only works in radians. Convert: 1 rotation = 2π rad = 360°.

questions.prompt: A wheel of radius 0.3 m turns through 4 rad. How far does a point on its rim travel?
questions.explanation: s = rθ = 0.3 × 4 = 1.2 m. Stretched out, the arc is just a 1D distance.

questions.prompt: Using the class convention, a wheel spinning clockwise has an angular velocity that is:
questions.explanation: Counterclockwise is positive and clockwise negative, just like left being negative in 1D.

questions.prompt: To get the most torque from a wrench, push at what angle to the handle?
questions.explanation: |τ| = rF sin θ is largest when sin θ = 1. At 0° or 180° you push along the handle and get no torque.

questions.prompt: A rod with the same mass and length can spin about its center or about one end. Which is easier to spin up?
questions.explanation: More mass far from the axis means a bigger I. About the end, I is 4× bigger, so the same torque gives ¼ the α.

questions.prompt: A fan spinning at 50 rad/s is switched off and stops in 10 s. What is its angular acceleration?
questions.explanation: α = (0 − 50)/10 = −5 rad/s², negative because it slows down.

questions.prompt: A fan slows steadily from 50 rad/s to 0 in 10 s. Through what angle does it turn while stopping?
A wheel turns at a steady 7.5 rad/s for 60 s. How many rotations is that?
questions.explanation: Δθ = 7.5 × 60 = 450 rad, and 450/2π = 71.6 rotations.

questions.prompt: You pull a door handle 0.8 m from the hinge with 30 N, at 60° to the door. What torque do you apply?
A 2 kg ring of radius 0.5 m (I = mr²) gets a net torque of 3 N·m. What is its angular acceleration?
questions.explanation: I = 2 × 0.5² = 0.5 kg·m², so α = τ/I = 6 rad/s².

questions.prompt: Why don't you give a direction for energy (like "75 J North")?
choices: Only kinetic energy has a direction
questions.explanation: Energy has size only, so energy problems need no components, which is why they are often easier than kinematics.

questions.prompt: 1 joule equals:
questions.explanation: ½mv² has units kg·(m/s)² = kg·m²/s². kg·m/s² is a newton, kg·m/s is momentum.

questions.prompt: A 1 kg ball and a 10 kg ball are dropped from the same height (no air resistance). Which is moving faster at the ground?
questions.explanation: mgh = ½mv²: m cancels, v = √(2gh). The heavy ball has more energy, but not more speed.

questions.prompt: Energy conservation gives the speed at the bottom of a ramp. What can't it tell you?
choices: The kinetic energy at the bottom
questions.explanation: Energy has no time in it. For time you still need kinematics.

questions.prompt: If a car's speed doubles, its kinetic energy:
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv²: 2× speed gives 2² = 4× the energy, which is also 4× the braking distance.

questions.prompt: What is the kinetic energy of a 1200 kg car moving at 15 m/s?
A 55 kg climber goes up 120 m. How much gravitational potential energy does she gain? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A water balloon is dropped from rest 20 m up. How fast is it going just before it hits the ground? (g = 9.8 m/s², no air resistance)
A spring with k = 800 N/m is compressed 0.10 m. How much energy does it store?
questions.explanation: ½kx² = ½ × 800 × 0.10² = 4 J. Forgetting to square x gives 40.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg puck slides at 6 m/s onto a floor with μk = 0.2. How far does it go before stopping? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.explanation: All of ½mv² = 72 J goes into friction work μk·mg·d = 7.84d, so d = 9.18 m. (In the blueprint's Example 23, part b works out to 23.4 m/s; it rounds down to 23.3.)

questions.prompt: An object is in static equilibrium when:
choices: It moves at a constant speed
questions.explanation: Zero net force keeps it from sliding, zero net torque keeps it from spinning. You need both.

questions.prompt: Two kids of equal mass sit on a seesaw. Where must they sit to balance it?
choices: At equal distances from the pivot
Both at the very ends, wherever the pivot is
questions.answer: At equal distances from the pivot
questions.explanation: Torque is weight × distance; equal weights need equal distances.

questions.prompt: For torque, where does a uniform beam's weight act?
choices: Nowhere: a beam's weight makes no torque
questions.explanation: A uniform beam acts as if all its weight sits at its middle, which makes torque whenever the pivot isn't there.

questions.prompt: A 30 kg kid sits 2 m left of a seesaw's pivot. Where must a 40 kg kid sit to balance? (distance right of the pivot; ignore the board's weight)
questions.explanation: 30 × 2 = 40 × d → d = 1.5 m. The heavier kid sits closer.

questions.prompt: A 15 kg board balances on one pivot with a 30 kg kid and a 45 kg kid on it. How hard does the pivot push up? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Net force = 0: (15 + 30 + 45) × 9.8 = 882 N. Don't forget the board.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg weight hangs 0.4 m left of a balance's pivot. What mass hung 0.6 m right of the pivot keeps it level?
A uniform 10 kg beam, 4 m long, rests on a pivot 1 m from its left end. What mass hung at the left end keeps it level?
questions.explanation: The beam's weight acts at its center, 2 m from the left end, so 1 m right of the pivot. m × 1 = 10 × 1 → m = 10 kg.

formulas.name: Sig figs
formulas.formula: Nonzero digits count; captive zeros count; leading zeros never; trailing zeros only with a decimal point

formulas.name: Scientific notation
formulas.note: keep exactly the sig figs in a

formulas.name: Displacement
formulas.note: signed; distance is the path length

formulas.name: Graphs
formulas.formula: x-t slope = v;  v-t slope = a;  v-t area = Δx

formulas.name: Components
formulas.formula: Ax = A cos θ,  Ay = A sin θ
formulas.note: θ from the +x axis; from N/S, swap sin and cos

formulas.name: Adding
formulas.formula: Rx = Ax + Bx + …,  Ry = Ay + By + …

formulas.name: Launch components
formulas.formula: v₀x = v₀ cos θ,  v₀y = v₀ sin θ

formulas.name: Vertical
formulas.formula: Δy = v₀y t − ½(9.8)t²,  v_y = v₀y − 9.8t

formulas.name: Fall time (horizontal launch)
formulas.note: only the height sets the time

formulas.name: Static friction
formulas.note: matches the push up to its max

formulas.name: Incline
formulas.formula: F_N = mg cos θ,  along the ramp mg sin θ

formulas.name: Rotational kinematics
formulas.formula: ω = ω₀ + αt,  Δθ = ω₀t + ½αt²,  ω² = ω₀² + 2αΔθ

formulas.name: Moments of inertia
formulas.formula: rod (center) mL²/12;  rod (end) mL²/3;  ring mr²;  sphere ⅖mr²

formulas.name: Uniform beam
formulas.formula: its weight acts at its center
